If AI is so great, why aren’t we seeing an explosion of new, amazing software products? If anyone can turn their idea into working software with coding agents, where is all that software ? People have been asking this question for years. As far as I can tell, the answer is that it’s spread out over a lot of modestly successful projects:

- Somewhere between 2x and 20x new software is being created, depending on where you look

- There’s no real growth in massively successful software projects (not counting AI tools)

- There is around 2x growth in modestly successful software projects

### Where all the new software is

I picked 1 around twenty separate sources — software marketplaces, plugin registries, modding platforms, etc — which expose installation counts. I then compared the number 2 of successful software projects between 2022-24 and 2025-26: i.e. before and after agentic coding hit the mainstream in mid-2025.

There’s a clear jump in modestly (not wildly) successful projects. For instance, the NVDA screen-reader addons directory had a bit over twice as many new addons with more than a thousand downloads (though no change in addons with more than ten thousand). The HACS open-source home automation community plugins store likewise saw twice as many new addons with over a hundred installs but no change in ones with over a thousand. New Steam games with over a hundred reviews are about 60% more common now than pre-2024. Obsidian plugins, Firefox and Chrome extensions, Nexus game mods, and Blender extensions had the same pattern. The Google Play store, WordPress plugins, and a few others didn’t show this pattern, but I think it’s still enough to conclude that AI is indeed driving a boom in hobbyist software.

### Why addons and plugins?

I think examining addons, mods, and plugins is useful for a few reasons. First, it’s usually pretty easy to tell how many people are using them, or at least have installed them. Obviously AI is letting people produce a lot of software — I work at GitHub, so I see this first-hand — but without checking installation counts it’s unclear how much of this is actually being used.

Second, it’s a good way to minimize the amount of software that’s about AI . It doesn’t tell us much about AI’s effect on software to point out all the successful software projects that help people code with AI. That’s just selling shovels. The real question is whether AI is helping generate software that solves people’s ordinary problems .

AI-generated game mods and ports are a great example of this, because gamers aren’t trying to change the world with AI coding. They just want to play multiplayer Halo CE in the browser, or fly a plane in Helldivers, or play Super Smash online with rollback netcode. It’s looking like 3 AI can supply this need effectively.

### Were these projects actually AI generated?

Everyone is very coy about AI usage in hobbyist communities. In the rare cases where people admit it, they often get dogpiled. People really don’t like AI, even when it’s producing software they find useful. Given that, I don’t think it’s possible to use voluntary AI disclosure data to figure out whether AI is driving a software boom: the presence of the tag itself will discourage use, and many developers are just not going to admit it.

A 2x growth in successful projects between 2022-24 and 2025-26 is clearly something to do with AI, particularly in the background of a 10x growth in total projects. Of course not all of these projects will have AI involvement. But when people ask “why hasn’t AI improved software”, they’re talking about a missing trend 4 : wondering where all the new software is. As it turns out, it’s going towards a lot of small software projects that a few hundred or thousand people find useful.

### Why small, moderately successful projects?

Why is AI growth visible in small projects but not big software companies? Why is it concentrated in moderately successful products and not wildly successful ones? I don’t have any data for this, but here’s my speculation.

Big, successful software companies often have all the visible features they want. That’s why there’s not a wild explosion of new features in, say, macOS or Gmail: what would those features even be? As I’ve written about before , they’re also technically paralyzed by the features they have, so it’s not trivial for even very good coding agents to add new ones. Finally, many new features in successful products are subtle (e.g. enterprise compatibility things that almost all users will never encounter, or purely internal systems that slightly increase reliability).

It’s less clear to me why there aren’t many new wildly successful hobbyist projects. Maybe it’s just hard to have a really good idea for a product, and AI can’t help with that. Or maybe it takes years for a really successful project to develop, and we need to be patient for the current crop of thousand-user tools to grow into hundred-thousand-user tools.

Many people think 1 that getting “good at AI” is trivial. Sure, with some early models there were tricks you had to learn, 2 but current models don’t need them. Even if there are different tricks 3 that work on current models, the next generation will render them obsolete, so why bother? Just tell the model what you want it to do.

This take is particularly popular with the anti-AI crowd, who scoff 4 at the idea that AI-reluctant people are being left behind, or that it might be irresponsible to advise other engineers to avoid AI use entirely. According to them, if AI does ever become capable enough to be worth using, they’ll be able to start using it with no learning curve. Is that right?

No. Like most things, getting good at using AI isn’t just about clever tricks. It requires developing long-term skills 5 , which takes time and practice.

### Supplying the right context

One failure mode I’ve seen with people who are new to AI is expecting it to read their mind: for instance, asking it to “solve my issue” without ever saying what the issue is, or asking it about some Slack-related problem without actually connecting your agent to Slack. Agents are flexible and will try their absolute hardest to guess what problem you’re facing and how to solve it, but the guesses will be largely wrong. Skilled AI users will pick up on the fact that the agent is missing key context and backtrack.

Skilled AI users will also reflexively include why they want to achieve their current goal, so that the agent has enough context to make decisions. This is often non-trivial: most of us know what we want to do but have to take a second to think about the broader reasons behind it.

### Knowing what the model can and can’t do

AI capabilities are weird : they are very good at some tasks and very bad at others, and it’s hard to predict which task falls into which category. For instance, I know that I can ask an agent to come up with new architectural ideas for how to structure a service, but that I shouldn’t ask it to come up with new features that the service can offer. Worse still, there is a third category 6 of tasks that AI models are bad at but can be prompted into being good: for instance, writing PR descriptions.

Of course, this changes with new models, but less than you’d think. In general, new models get much better at the tasks the old models were already good at, and a little better at the tasks the old models sucked at. So developing a sense of what AI can and can’t do is a surprisingly durable skill.

Really internalizing what the model can do is trickier than it sounds. For instance, I initially struggled to set up MCP servers for GitHub Copilot before realizing 7 I could just ask Copilot to install its own MCP servers. I now reflexively ask AI agents to do local testing of changes — standing up servers, hammering them with curls, running through variations and edge cases — but it took me a while to realize I could ask for that. I have only just started scheduling a job for 6am my time for an agent to go through messages that have come in from different timezones and do some preliminary investigation. What other capabilities 8 am I leaving on the table?

### Knowing what mistakes the models make

Reviewing AI-generated code is a substantially different skillset from reviewing human-written code. There are whole categories of bugs — off-by-one errors, for instance — that human-written code is prone to but AI-generated code is not. Similarly, there are mistakes that are rare in human-written code but are very common in AI-generated code. I’ve written about how these tend to be mistakes of misalignment : over-engineering some areas that humans would know aren’t important, or trading off important requirements in order to satisfy made-up ones, and so on.

Reviewers used to human-written code are often dazzled by the superficial fluency of AI-generated code. It’s always exhaustively commented and tested and uses sophisticated language features. If a human programmer produced code like this, you’d be inclined to trust their judgment that a mutex is required in this case — but with an AI programmer, you ought to be very suspicious about new mutexes, which are often introduced to satisfy completely insignificant edge cases.

### Rapidly skim-reading AI slop

This skill is kind of silly, but it’s so practically important I have to include it. AI models produce a lot of useful output, but it’s often lost in a thick forest of verbiage. Once you’ve read enough of it, you can sort of just let your eyes flow over the phrasing until you get to the specific claims and evidence. If you’re not used to this, you will waste a lot of time and emotional energy trying to cut through the foliage.

### Will these skills be made obsolete too?

It’s possible that these skills are also temporary. Maybe in the future the agent will just do what we want perfectly, freeing us from the need to actually read its output. Maybe model tooling will get good enough to automatically supply the right context, and the models will get good enough to be able to do everything and make no mistakes. Maybe! But that would require the models to get so good that humans aren’t needed at all.

Don’t be a doomer. Like chess, software’s centaur age — the period where a human-machine pairing can beat individual humans or machines — may last decades . Developing skills for the centaur age is still worthwhile, just like it was worthwhile to learn Angular or React even though it seemed likely that those frameworks would be obsolete 9 in a decade.

### Conclusion

I’ve left a lot of skills out: knowing when to abandon or steer an agent session, how to break work up between agents, when to trust AI claims and when to verify, how to minimize costs by using smaller models, and so on. On top of all that, even though it’s not durably useful to stay up to date with the current set of tricks (plus knowing which model is the best for which tasks), it’s still very useful in the short-term. Keeping up without getting lost is a skill in its own right.

It shouldn’t be surprising that working with AI involves actual skills. It’s like working with a really weird person: a savant with mad skills in some areas and huge gaps in others, a prolific but inexpert communicator, a workaholic with no long-term memory, and so on. If you were a manager and had someone like that as your employee, you could likely get a lot of value out of them, but it would take time 10 to figure out how.

If you’re deliberately avoiding using AI, you are likely being left behind by the people who aren’t. If you’re advising other people to avoid AI completely, you are doing them no favors. I do think it’s a mistake to go fully into AI, because LLMs reward expertise , which is best gained by hand. However, if you never practice using AI, you are never going to get good at it.

> Tell agents the why, not just the how Early AI agents were basically enthusiastic idiots. Working with them required you to tell them precisely what you wanted them to do (for instance, “method A exists on class B, please add an equivalent method to classes C through F”). Otherwise they’d go off and do entirely the wrong thing. But as AI agents have improved, this has changed. When frontier models go off and do the wrong thing today, they don’t do it because they’re confused, they do it because they make an incorrect assumption about your goals or priorities. For instance, when GPT-6-Astra thinks it’s writing code for itself, it will produce minified code . It’s perfectly capable of writing human-readable code — at least in Golang, where I’ve produced several thousand lines of acceptable code with the model — but you have to tell it that humans will be reading the code.
